Wendy Thienes Local Journalism Initiative Reporter The Shaunavon Standard Shaunavon’s First World War in 12 Objects The Grand Coteau Heritage & Cultural Centre (GCHCC) will showcase a unique exhibit of World War I items made available to them through Western University in London, Ontario. Every year the University utilizes the Ley and Lois Smith Collection in the History Department at the University to undertake a project to raise awareness of Remembrance Day by sharing some of its treasures with people across Canada. Professor of History Jonathan Vance approached the Grand Coteau about the project, inviting the Centre to display “Shaunavon’s First World War in 12 Objects” to supplement their own plans to mark Remembrance Day. Twelve selected items from the Smith Collection that connect to Shaunavon’s experience in the First World War include postcards and photos, carefully curated to give a sense of the war’s impact on Shaunavon and surrounding area. Vance explains the project includes displays for 50 or 60 communities across Canada. “Our plan with this project was to connect with local museums and libraries that might not have much in the way of archival material in their collections, or might not have the staff resources to put something together. Essentially, we wanted to do some of the work for them. We would provide a number of objects from our own collection, along with the explanatory texts and the basic structure of an exhibit. The institutions could either use that material as-is, or just pop in things from their own collection to build an even larger display.” GCHCC’s Collections Manager Kelly Attrell says, “Shaunavon-related archival material can be found in museums and archives across Canada, but unless you know where to look and what you’re looking for, it can be hard for researchers to locate. We’re very happy that Professor Vance reached out to us and is allowing us to share this presentation.” Attrell explains that the images will be printed for viewing and a slide show of the images is being created that can be viewed at the Centre and online via their webpage on the Town of Shaunavon’s website. Text accompanying the postcard images from Western University explains, “Soldiers overseas relied on mail to maintain connections with home, and the military in turn devoted significant resources to ensuring that postcards and letters travelled safely. Each piece of mail was censored at least three times before entering the civilian postal system: once by an officer in the soldier’s unit (the signature in the upper left-hand corner); then by a field censor just behind the front lines (the black circle under the stamp); and finally by a military censor closer to England (the red hexagon in the upper left-hand corner).” A form style postcard, the Field Service Postcard, was eventually introduced. Also known as the Whizz-Bang, it was created to reduce the burden imposed by the need to censor all mail leaving the war zone and therefore reached home more quickly than a normal letter. Archival material indicates that more than 110 men enlisted in Shaunavon for the 209th Battalion in 1916, although local newspaper archives indicate that ‘200 soldiers from Shaunavon were on their way to summer camp…’. Some of these men were from the surrounding region, not only Shaunavon. One photo in the collection is of a soldier from the 209th Battalion but his identity is not known. Some names mentioned within the archival material include people that long-time Shaunavon residents may have heard of, even though the First World War ended 107 years ago. One postcard recipient was Frank Bransted of Shaunavon who would eventually be a dedicated volunteer of the Grand Coteau Museum circa 1931. Minnesota native Martin Irgens wrote to Bransted. Irgens was a farm labourer in Frontier, Saskatchewan, when he was conscripted in January 1918. Three months later, he was in England, and three months after that, he was on the fighting lines in France. According to this postcard sent to Bransted in Shaunavon, he was not happy about the speed with which he was shipped out of Canada. En route Feb 13 – 1918 Friend Frank: Am in route overseas they wouldn’t give us a leave to go home. It was a pretty rotten deal they give us. If you can make anything on those books, just help yourself. Sorry I couldn’t get home. I would have sure sent you the money. My best regards to all in Shaunavon. Martin Irgens “Fat” Shaunavon ex-soldiers Joseph Hossie, a lawyer who had served in the artillery, and accountant Thomas Stothers, a veteran of the Canadian Machine Gun Corps, are featured as contributors known as The ‘Wheeze Bangs’, in a veterans magazine, The Rum Jar. The nickname is an obvious play on words of the aforementioned Whizz Bang postcard. Hossie also has ties to the Grand Coteau Museum, serving as its Vice President in 1931. Other Shaunavon and area surnames mentioned that may be gone but not forgotten include Roy (Louis Roy of Dollard) and Ellis (Gordon) of Shaunavon. Professor Vance explains the goals of creating an exhibition of this nature. “On one level, I want people to know that each community’s experience with the First World War was unique and important – we can only really understand the war on a national level if we know how it was experienced locally. Second, I want people to know that there are historians out here in Ontario who are interested in Shaunavon’s First World War experience – and the war experience of countless other small communities! Finally, I’d like people to think about their community now and how it connects to that war. Do they recognize some of the names in the material? Are there Great War veterans in their own family that they could learn more about? Do they have letters, photos, or artifacts from their family that might go to a museum or archive, where they could be safeguarded and used to understand the history?” Attrell says the archival items will also be printed off for closer viewing and World War I artifacts from the Centre’s own collection will be on display to augment the exhibition. Attrell invites visitors to stop by to view the exhibition or to visit the Centre’s webpage on the Town of Shaunavon website to view the YouTube video. The Centre is open Tuesday-Friday from 9 am – 5 pm. They are closed on November 11, but visitors can see this display until November 14. At Collider, he writes features and reviews, and has interviewed the cast and crew of Dark Winds . In addition to writing about stories, Michael has told a few of his own. Based on the novel of the same name by Philipp Meyer , the Western drama follows Pierce Brosnan \'s "first son of Texas" Eli McCullough as he seeks to secure his family\'s legacy in the Lone Star State, no matter who stands in his way. A well-rounded and intense take on the genre, The Son deals with multiple time periods within Texan history as the McCulloughs fight desperately (and often unfairly) for their livelihood and legacy. \'The Son\' Was \'Yellowstone\' Before Taylor Sheridan Took Over the TV Genre Pierce Brosnan as Eli McCullough at his desk on \'The Son\' Image via AMC Part of what has drawn so many in to Taylor Sheridan \'s Yellowstone franchise is that, although the flagship drama is a 21st-century neo-Western, the Dutton story has been explored further in prequels ( and upcoming spin-offs ) that emphasize how the Dutton empire rose in the first place. 1883 covers the original Montana branch of the family tree as they settle in the Last Best Place, while 1923 notes how they secured their home and fortune in the wake of greedy businessmen and a nationwide depression. But what truly sets The Son apart — which premiered on AMC over a year before Yellowstone first hit the Paramount Network — is that it blended two (and later three) time periods together to tell a sweeping Western epic over the span of 20 episodes . And with three fewer seasons than Yellowstone and no spin-offs to boot, it tells a fuller, more complete story about the harshness of the American West and the legacy of those who settled it than Sheridan ever could. Posts By Michael John Petty Aug 20, 2025 The Western genre has often waxed poetic about ideas of legacy and progress. Most modern takes on the genre emphasize the violence involved in not just winning the West , but conquering by any means necessary. By the time oil gets involved, things get even messier between the McCullough family and everyone who comes into their path. The Son tackles all the classic Western people groups , from the varying degrees of white settlers who make Texas their home to the warring Native American tribes and Mexican stragglers who attempt to assimilate on the northern side of the border. With characters to root for and despise on all sides of the conflict, this complicated AMC production is the natural successor to the network\'s previous horse opera, Hell on Wheels , while paving its own distinct path — even if there are several similarities to what audiences would later see on Yellowstone . Pierce Brosnan\'s Western Series \'The Son\' Explores 2 Distinct Time Periods of American History Pierce Brosnan as Eli McCullough wearing a grey vest and holding a gun in \'The Son.\' Image via Sonar Entertainment While Brosnan plays the tough-as-nails McCullough patriarch in the future, a man who is not to be trifled with and who could lose control at any moment (just look at Season 2\'s "Somebody Get a Shovel"), a younger Eli appears in the show\'s 1850s narrative played by future Landman star Jacob Lofland . Frankly, the young Eli plot is oftentimes more engaging than the 1915 story featuring Brosnan , if not simply because it leans more into the Western historical elements of Texas\' founding . After Eli\'s entire family is murdered by a band of Comanche, the young man is made a slave. But, over time, he becomes a Comanche himself, pursuing a romance with the intense Prairie Flower ( Elizabeth Frances ) and becoming a son of sorts to the chief Toshaway (the ever-impressive Zahn McClarnon ). If the statement "what\'s past is prologue" is true for any character, it\'s especially relevant for the older Eli McCullough, whose past clearly informs his present, giving us a deeper look at how he went from being a man of honor to one of Texas\' most fearsome colonels. Conversely, the 1915 story engages with a narrative that feels eerily like Yellowstone , though it arguably handles its characters and plot with far more care and intentionality. Eli is the John Dutton-like ( Kevin Costner ) patriarch, as we\'ve established, and just like the Dutton figurehead , he has two sons who are responsible for different functions of the family business — his older boy, Phineas ( David Wilson Barnes ), is the politically aspiring middle son, while his youngest, Pete ( Henry Garrett ), is the prodigal child who remains Eli\'s favorite, the one he wants to take over the ranch one day. Like the Duttons, the McCulloughs fend off neighboring rivals who would just as soon take the land back from them (in this case, the Mexican García family rather than a collection of Indian tribes), as well as outside parties interested in the land for its oil. It doesn\'t get more intense than this. Then we get to the third time period, which isn\'t introduced until the second and final season. Set in 1988, it follows an old Jeannie McCullough ( Lois Smith ), Eli\'s granddaughter, who eventually takes over the brand, serving as the last remaining McCullough of this patch of South Texas. Idolizing her grandfather, Jeannie interacts with a young ranch hand named Ulises Gonzales ( Alex Hernandez ), who remains quite curious about the famed Texan Colonel who built the empire that Jeannie so comfortably enjoys. The way their story ends is a powerful one, concluding The Son saga with a new son who aims to take back the land and legacy by bridging the gap between two rivals . \'The Son\' Is a Gritty Western That Gets a Satisfying Ending The biggest tragedy of The Son is that AMC axed the Western series too soon . After the first 10 episodes dropped in 2017, the Bronsan-led drama was quickly renewed by the network, but AMC quickly announced that Season 2 would be its final season as well. In 2019, the series ended with a climactic final episode that redefines the rest of the story, blurring the lines between the myth of the American West and the historical realities that founded it. It\'s the type of ending that is as complicated as it is satisfying, but one that you\'ll likely enjoy more than what Paramount would do years later with Yellowstone . The performances alone are well worth the 20-episode binge, as Pierce Brosnan commands the screen as the tortured and conflicted Eli McCullough , always trying to gain the upper hand on everyone around him. If there\'s one thing about The Son we wished would last just a little longer, it would be that we could see how the young Eli played by Lofland became the hardened cattle baron and oil tycoon we see him as at the end of his life. Although The Son explores some of that, there are so many years between 1952 and 1915 that we\'re left to fill in the blanks. Either way, the drama offers something a bit more satisfying than many modern Westerns that end before their time. The Son is available for streaming on AMC+. Col Kenneth D. Royer is seen in a picture from his military service. SPRING MILLS — For most of his life, Lt. Col. Kenneth D. Royer didn’t speak much about his time in the U.S. Air Force. It wasn’t until after his death in October of last year, when his sons opened an old military trunk, that they discovered the full scope of their father’s service, from flight maps from secret bombing runs and medals for valor to his meticulous notes from more than 240 combat missions. Royer, who was 91 when he died in 2024, was born in Centre Hall and spent much of his youth in nearby Millheim. A serious man who remained active in his community, Royer was notoriously private. In his later years, he suffered complications linked to Agent Orange, a hazardous tactical herbicide used in Vietnam, and carried with him the weight of the missions he had flown — particularly the traumatic loss of members of his flight crew. Despite his silence, Royer meticulously documented his service, leaving behind maps, photographs and hand-written notes tucked away in his home. HUNTER SMITH/THE EXPRESS Kenneth's sons, Donald and Dennis, are pictured amidst their father’s memorabilia. After his passing, his sons began sorting through the memorabilia and uncovered, among other things, evidence of covert bombing campaigns in Laos and Cambodia, as well as personal records that added depth to their understanding of his life. Kenneth Royer enlisted in the Air Force on April 7, 1953, and completed basic training at a military installation in New York, where he passed the Aviation Cadet Entrance Examination. Later that year, he graduated from Lackland Air Force Base in Texas and began what would become a decorated, two-decade-long career that took him from the Korean Peninsula to the skies over Vietnam. During his service, Royer served as a radar navigator on more than 240 B-52 bombing missions — a tally almost unheard of among airmen of his era. Known for his precision, he performed complex calculations amid enemy fire to guide his crew through successful strikes against critical targets. After one mission, his son Donald J. Royer recalled, “The military police came out in a Jeep, got him from the plane and took him back to a conference room. They went over what his next mission was and gave him a half-hour before getting into another B-52 and flying.” Royer’s skill as a navigator earned him the respect of his fellow crew members and made him indispensable to his squadron. HUNTER SMITH/THE EXPRESS Various photos, medals, journals and other artifacts uncovered by the Royer family after Kenneth passed on Oct. 11, 2024 are shown. “I asked him one time, I said, ‘So, you’re that good?'” Donald said. “And he goes, ‘You put a dime in the backyard, guarantee I’ll hit it.'” Royer’s skill and steadiness in the sky earned him a long list of decorations over his 20 years of service. A multiple-time recipient of the Air Medal — conferred by executive order of the president — he received one for each tour and notable accomplishment. Among his other honors were the Air Force Commendation Medal, Combat Readiness Medal, Good Conduct Medal, National Defense Service Medal, Korean Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, United Nations Medal, Republic of Vietnam Campaign Medal, Presidential Unit Citation, Air Force Outstanding Unit Award, Air Force Longevity Service Award Ribbon, Air Force Organizational Excellence Award, and the Small Arms Expert Marksmanship Ribbon, among others. But his most prestigious honor came in 1972, when he was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross. On April 4 of that year, Royer demonstrated exceptional skill during aerial operations as a B-52 radar navigator over Southeast Asia. “On that date, while flying a critical bombing mission against a high-priority target, Colonel Royer’s aircraft encountered hostile fire immediately after making a successful weapons release,” the citation accompanying the award reads. “During the attack, Colonel Royer constantly kept his pilot advised of missile detonations and other aircraft positions, thereby dynamically assisting in the safe recovery of all aircraft and crews.” HUNTER SMITH/THE EXPRESS Various photos, medals, journals and other artifacts uncovered by the Royer family after Kenneth passed on Oct. 11, 2024 are shown. The award goes on to highlight his skill and dedication: “The professional competence, aerial skill and devotion to duty displayed by Colonel Royer reflect great credit upon himself and the United States Air Force.” “He got everybody back safe by keeping them apprised as to what was going on and where they were at,” said his daughter-in-law, Penny Royer, proudly. Though he was most well-regarded as a radar navigator, “the other aspect of his military career is that most of it was in the Strategic Air Command,” said one of his other sons, Dennis D. Royer. Throughout the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union held their fingers over the proverbial nuclear button. At each base, Dennis said, about six planes were usually pre-loaded with nuclear weapons. As part of his responsibilities, his father was prepared to respond to a nuclear attack at a moment’s notice. Dennis, who lived on base with his father, recalled one of the tensest moments of that era: the Cuban Missile Crisis. HUNTER SMITH/THE EXPRESS Various photos, medals, journals and other artifacts uncovered by the Royer family after Kenneth passed on Oct. 11, 2024 are shown. “During the Cuban Missile Crisis, they were at the end of the runway — engines running — waiting for takeoff,” he said. “What their targets were, who knows. But they were ready to wage nuclear war.” Thankfully, the U.S. and the Soviet Union didn’t come to blows, and Royer was able to conclude his career alive, having never deployed a nuclear weapon. Instead, near the end of his career, he reached a personal milestone: his 200th mission, when his wife, Lois Smith, joined him in the tower. “They were soulmates,” said Penny. “She was his driving force.” On that mission, Penny said. “She got on the radio and said, ‘Honey, I’m bringing you home.'” Having preceded him in death, Lois, Penny imagines, offered the same guidance on his final journey to the heavens that she gave him on his way down from them. (Image Via: CBS) Elsbeth Season 3 is back with another wild mystery, and Episode 5, \'Poetic Justice,\' might just be the best one yet. This time, Elsbeth crosses paths with the elite poetry crowd of New York, only to uncover a chilling murder hidden behind rhymes and egos. The episode features some brilliant guest stars, including The Good Place ’s William Jackson Harper as the killer of the week. So, who are the faces behind Elsbeth Season 3 Episode 5’s smartest and sneakiest characters? Let’s break it down. When Poetry Meets Murder: Inside Elsbeth Season 3 Episode 5 Episode 5 of Elsbeth Season 3 is aptly titled \'Poetic Justice.\' The episode opens with Elsbeth Tascioni attending a high-profile fundraiser, only to stumble upon a case that is as strange as it is high profile. The plot of the episode centers around Gary Pidgeon, played by William Jackson Harper, a rich guy who runs a struggling poetry journal called Pidgeon Press. His tag line, “ The arts are under attack! ” sets the tone for his desperation and also ultimately, his downfall. Gary’s troubles start when a wealthy donor, Dolores Feinn (played by Lois Smith), threatens to cut him off after he refuses to publish her bizarre, self-centered poem. What follows is a darkly comedic twist as Gary kills her by manipulating her oxygen tank and letting her literally “ignite” her own end. Harper’s calm intensity and quiet panic give the character layers that make this episode a standout in Elsbeth Season 3. Meanwhile, Elsbeth runs into her old friend Marissa Gold (Sarah Steele), now working on a political campaign for Alec Bloom (Ivan Hernandez). Their reunion adds a whole lot of nostalgia for longtime fans who remember The Good Wife . Elsbeth’s accidental involvement in Marissa’s campaign plans, all thanks to a “fake date” gone wrong, becomes a subplot that is equal parts funny and awkward, showing off Carrie Preston’s brilliant comedic timing. The Elsbeth Season 3 Episode 5 Cast and Character Guide Carrie Preston as Elsbeth Tascioni: Carrie Preston once again proves she is Elsbeth Tascioni. Her chaotic brilliance makes her one of the most watchable leads on TV right now. In Elsbeth Season 3, she is still working alongside the NYPD, using her quirky logic to see connections no one else can. 78th Annual Tony Awards - Arrivals - Source: Getty In Episode 5, she pieces together the murder by noticing the faintest detail, like the discoloration on a tweed jacket. Preston’s performance balances humor and humanity, especially in her scenes with Alec Bloom, where the chemistry is undeniable. Carrie Preston is also known for: The Good Wife & True Blood Wendell Pierce as Captain C.W. Wagner As Captain Wagner, Wendell Pierce continues to ground the show. His fatherly frustration with his detectives (and Elsbeth’s unpredictability) gives the series some of its funniest moments. 2025 Atlantic Festival - Source: Getty In Poetic Justice , he tries to keep the precinct from spinning into chaos while also managing his daughter Julia’s blossoming romance with Detective Rivers. Pierce reminds us that beneath the stern exterior, Wagner genuinely trusts Elsbeth’s instincts, even if she drives him up the wall. Wendell Pierce is also known for: The Wire & Suits Carra Patterson as Kaya Blanke Carra Patterson makes a special guest return as Kaya Blanke, and her comeback is a treat for longtime fans. Kaya started as Elsbeth’s NYPD observer and quickly became her confidante. CBS Fall Schedule Celebration - Source: Getty After being promoted to detective and later joining a task force in Washington, D.C., her brief reappearance in Elsbeth Season 3 feels like a homecoming. She pops up in Episode 5 to lend her perspective on the case, reminding us how much her calm logic used to balance Elsbeth’s own life. Carra Patterson is also known for: The Arrangement & Turner & Hooch Fredric Lehne as Lieutenant Dave Noonan Fredric Lehne’s Lieutenant Dave Noonan continues to bring that classic police procedural energy to the show. Noonan is dependable and straightforward and is the kind of guy who cuts through Elsbeth’s eccentric methods with simple logic. GBK & Pilot Pen\'s Luxury Style Lounge During New York Fashion Week - Day 2 - Source: Getty Though he is more in the background this episode, his steady presence keeps the precinct running smoothly. His interactions with Captain Wagner often add dry humor, giving Elsbeth Season 3 a touch of old-school detective grit. Fredric Lehne is also known for: Dream Lover & Amityville 4: The Evil Escapes William Jackson Harper as Gary Pidgeon William Jackson Harper absolutely steals Poetic Justice . As Gary Pidgeon, the editor of a once-prestigious poetry journal, Harper perfectly captures a man collapsing under the weight of ambition and pride. "Uncle Vanya" Opening Night - Source: Getty His calmness hides a rage that comes off only when Elsbeth exposes him. It’s a clever, eerie role that lets Harper show off his full acting range. William Jackson Harper is also known for: The Good Place & Midsommar Sarah Steele as Marissa Gold Sarah Steele’s return as Marissa Gold is pure nostalgia for The Good Wife fans. Now a campaign manager for mayoral candidate Alec Bloom, Marissa’s energy adds a political spin to Elsbeth Season 3. CBS\' "Elsbeth" Season 3 Premiere - Source: Getty Her scheming, like setting up Elsbeth on a fake date for PR, goes hilariously off track. By the end, her confession that she leaked the “mysterious redhead” photos shows her bold, slightly mischievous side. Steele plays Marissa with perfect comedic timing, proving she is still as sharp as ever. Sarah Steele is also known for: The Good Fight & Speech & Debate Elsbeth Season 3 Episode 5, \'Poetic Justice,\' has, like always, chaotic politics and murder in the most Elsbeth way possible. With Carrie Preston’s charm, William Jackson Harper’s gripping guest role, and Sarah Steele’s (guest) return, this episode stands tall among the season’s best. Every character adds their spark to the story, and it is proof that Elsbeth Season 3 knows how to turn even poetry into the perfect crime. Wendy Thienes Local Journalism Initiative Reporter The Shaunavon Standard Shaunavon’s First World War in 12 Objects The Grand Coteau Heritage & Cultural Centre (GCHCC) will showcase a unique exhibit of World War I items made available to them through Western University in London, Ontario. Every year the University utilizes the Ley and Lois Smith Collection in the History Department at the University to undertake a project to raise awareness of Remembrance Day by sharing some of its treasures with people across Canada. Professor of History Jonathan Vance approached the Grand Coteau about the project, inviting the Centre to display “Shaunavon’s First World War in 12 Objects” to supplement their own plans to mark Remembrance Day. Twelve selected items from the Smith Collection that connect to Shaunavon’s experience in the First World War include postcards and photos, carefully curated to give a sense of the war’s impact on Shaunavon and surrounding area. Vance explains the project includes displays for 50 or 60 communities across Canada. “Our plan with this project was to connect with local museums and libraries that might not have much in the way of archival material in their collections, or might not have the staff resources to put something together. Essentially, we wanted to do some of the work for them. We would provide a number of objects from our own collection, along with the explanatory texts and the basic structure of an exhibit. The institutions could either use that material as-is, or just pop in things from their own collection to build an even larger display.” GCHCC’s Collections Manager Kelly Attrell says, “Shaunavon-related archival material can be found in museums and archives across Canada, but unless you know where to look and what you’re looking for, it can be hard for researchers to locate. We’re very happy that Professor Vance reached out to us and is allowing us to share this presentation.” Attrell explains that the images will be printed for viewing and a slide show of the images is being created that can be viewed at the Centre and online via their webpage on the Town of Shaunavon’s website. Text accompanying the postcard images from Western University explains, “Soldiers overseas relied on mail to maintain connections with home, and the military in turn devoted significant resources to ensuring that postcards and letters travelled safely. Each piece of mail was censored at least three times before entering the civilian postal system: once by an officer in the soldier’s unit (the signature in the upper left-hand corner); then by a field censor just behind the front lines (the black circle under the stamp); and finally by a military censor closer to England (the red hexagon in the upper left-hand corner).” A form style postcard, the Field Service Postcard, was eventually introduced. Also known as the Whizz-Bang, it was created to reduce the burden imposed by the need to censor all mail leaving the war zone and therefore reached home more quickly than a normal letter. Archival material indicates that more than 110 men enlisted in Shaunavon for the 209th Battalion in 1916, although local newspaper archives indicate that ‘200 soldiers from Shaunavon were on their way to summer camp…’. Some of these men were from the surrounding region, not only Shaunavon. One photo in the collection is of a soldier from the 209th Battalion but his identity is not known. Some names mentioned within the archival material include people that long-time Shaunavon residents may have heard of, even though the First World War ended 107 years ago. One postcard recipient was Frank Bransted of Shaunavon who would eventually be a dedicated volunteer of the Grand Coteau Museum circa 1931. Minnesota native Martin Irgens wrote to Bransted. Irgens was a farm labourer in Frontier, Saskatchewan, when he was conscripted in January 1918. Three months later, he was in England, and three months after that, he was on the fighting lines in France. According to this postcard sent to Bransted in Shaunavon, he was not happy about the speed with which he was shipped out of Canada. En route Feb 13 – 1918 Friend Frank: Am in route overseas they wouldn’t give us a leave to go home. It was a pretty rotten deal they give us. If you can make anything on those books, just help yourself. Sorry I couldn’t get home. I would have sure sent you the money. My best regards to all in Shaunavon. Martin Irgens “Fat” Shaunavon ex-soldiers Joseph Hossie, a lawyer who had served in the artillery, and accountant Thomas Stothers, a veteran of the Canadian Machine Gun Corps, are featured as contributors known as The ‘Wheeze Bangs’, in a veterans magazine, The Rum Jar. The nickname is an obvious play on words of the aforementioned Whizz Bang postcard. Hossie also has ties to the Grand Coteau Museum, serving as its Vice President in 1931. Other Shaunavon and area surnames mentioned that may be gone but not forgotten include Roy (Louis Roy of Dollard) and Ellis (Gordon) of Shaunavon. Professor Vance explains the goals of creating an exhibition of this nature. “On one level, I want people to know that each community’s experience with the First World War was unique and important – we can only really understand the war on a national level if we know how it was experienced locally. Second, I want people to know that there are historians out here in Ontario who are interested in Shaunavon’s First World War experience – and the war experience of countless other small communities! Finally, I’d like people to think about their community now and how it connects to that war. Do they recognize some of the names in the material? Are there Great War veterans in their own family that they could learn more about? Do they have letters, photos, or artifacts from their family that might go to a museum or archive, where they could be safeguarded and used to understand the history?” Attrell says the archival items will also be printed off for closer viewing and World War I artifacts from the Centre’s own collection will be on display to augment the exhibition. Attrell invites visitors to stop by to view the exhibition or to visit the Centre’s webpage on the Town of Shaunavon website to view the YouTube video. The Centre is open Tuesday-Friday from 9 am – 5 pm. They are closed on November 11, but visitors can see this display until November 14. Based on the novel of the same name by Philipp Meyer , the Western drama follows Pierce Brosnan \'s "first son of Texas" Eli McCullough as he seeks to secure his family\'s legacy in the Lone Star State, no matter who stands in his way. A well-rounded and intense take on the genre, The Son deals with multiple time periods within Texan history as the McCulloughs fight desperately (and often unfairly) for their livelihood and legacy. \'The Son\' Was \'Yellowstone\' Before Taylor Sheridan Took Over the TV Genre Pierce Brosnan as Eli McCullough at his desk on \'The Son\' Image via AMC Part of what has drawn so many in to Taylor Sheridan \'s Yellowstone franchise is that, although the flagship drama is a 21st-century neo-Western, the Dutton story has been explored further in prequels ( and upcoming spin-offs ) that emphasize how the Dutton empire rose in the first place. 1883 covers the original Montana branch of the family tree as they settle in the Last Best Place, while 1923 notes how they secured their home and fortune in the wake of greedy businessmen and a nationwide depression. But what truly sets The Son apart — which premiered on AMC over a year before Yellowstone first hit the Paramount Network — is that it blended two (and later three) time periods together to tell a sweeping Western epic over the span of 20 episodes . And with three fewer seasons than Yellowstone and no spin-offs to boot, it tells a fuller, more complete story about the harshness of the American West and the legacy of those who settled it than Sheridan ever could. Related Before He Joins Taylor Sheridan\'s Next Yellowstone Spin-Off, Watch Logan Marshall-Green\'s Underseen Western Series The actor\'s set to play Kayce Dutton\'s friend from the military. Posts By Michael John Petty Aug 20, 2025 The Western genre has often waxed poetic about ideas of legacy and progress. Most modern takes on the genre emphasize the violence involved in not just winning the West , but conquering by any means necessary. By the time oil gets involved, things get even messier between the McCullough family and everyone who comes into their path. The Son tackles all the classic Western people groups , from the varying degrees of white settlers who make Texas their home to the warring Native American tribes and Mexican stragglers who attempt to assimilate on the northern side of the border. With characters to root for and despise on all sides of the conflict, this complicated AMC production is the natural successor to the network\'s previous horse opera, Hell on Wheels , while paving its own distinct path — even if there are several similarities to what audiences would later see on Yellowstone . Pierce Brosnan\'s Western Series \'The Son\' Explores 2 Distinct Time Periods of American History Pierce Brosnan as Eli McCullough wearing a grey vest and holding a gun in \'The Son.\' Image via Sonar Entertainment While Brosnan plays the tough-as-nails McCullough patriarch in the future, a man who is not to be trifled with and who could lose control at any moment (just look at Season 2\'s "Somebody Get a Shovel"), a younger Eli appears in the show\'s 1850s narrative played by future Landman star Jacob Lofland . Frankly, the young Eli plot is oftentimes more engaging than the 1915 story featuring Brosnan , if not simply because it leans more into the Western historical elements of Texas\' founding . After Eli\'s entire family is murdered by a band of Comanche, the young man is made a slave. But, over time, he becomes a Comanche himself, pursuing a romance with the intense Prairie Flower ( Elizabeth Frances ) and becoming a son of sorts to the chief Toshaway (the ever-impressive Zahn McClarnon ). If the statement "what\'s past is prologue" is true for any character, it\'s especially relevant for the older Eli McCullough, whose past clearly informs his present, giving us a deeper look at how he went from being a man of honor to one of Texas\' most fearsome colonels. Conversely, the 1915 story engages with a narrative that feels eerily like Yellowstone , though it arguably handles its characters and plot with far more care and intentionality. Eli is the John Dutton-like ( Kevin Costner ) patriarch, as we\'ve established, and just like the Dutton figurehead , he has two sons who are responsible for different functions of the family business — his older boy, Phineas ( David Wilson Barnes ), is the politically aspiring middle son, while his youngest, Pete ( Henry Garrett ), is the prodigal child who remains Eli\'s favorite, the one he wants to take over the ranch one day. Like the Duttons, the McCulloughs fend off neighboring rivals who would just as soon take the land back from them (in this case, the Mexican García family rather than a collection of Indian tribes), as well as outside parties interested in the land for its oil. It doesn\'t get more intense than this. Then we get to the third time period, which isn\'t introduced until the second and final season. Set in 1988, it follows an old Jeannie McCullough ( Lois Smith ), Eli\'s granddaughter, who eventually takes over the brand, serving as the last remaining McCullough of this patch of South Texas. Idolizing her grandfather, Jeannie interacts with a young ranch hand named Ulises Gonzales ( Alex Hernandez ), who remains quite curious about the famed Texan Colonel who built the empire that Jeannie so comfortably enjoys. The way their story ends is a powerful one, concluding The Son saga with a new son who aims to take back the land and legacy by bridging the gap between two rivals . \'The Son\' Is a Gritty Western That Gets a Satisfying Ending The biggest tragedy of The Son is that AMC axed the Western series too soon . After the first 10 episodes dropped in 2017, the Bronsan-led drama was quickly renewed by the network, but AMC quickly announced that Season 2 would be its final season as well. In 2019, the series ended with a climactic final episode that redefines the rest of the story, blurring the lines between the myth of the American West and the historical realities that founded it. It\'s the type of ending that is as complicated as it is satisfying, but one that you\'ll likely enjoy more than what Paramount would do years later with Yellowstone . The performances alone are well worth the 20-episode binge, as Pierce Brosnan commands the screen as the tortured and conflicted Eli McCullough , always trying to gain the upper hand on everyone around him. If there\'s one thing about The Son we wished would last just a little longer, it would be that we could see how the young Eli played by Lofland became the hardened cattle baron and oil tycoon we see him as at the end of his life. Although The Son explores some of that, there are so many years between 1952 and 1915 that we\'re left to fill in the blanks. Either way, the drama offers something a bit more satisfying than many modern Westerns that end before their time. The Son is available for streaming on AMC+. Col Kenneth D. Royer is seen in a picture from his military service. SPRING MILLS — For most of his life, Lt. Col. Kenneth D. Royer didn’t speak much about his time in the U.S. Air Force. It wasn’t until after his death in October of last year, when his sons opened an old military trunk, that they discovered the full scope of their father’s service, from flight maps from secret bombing runs and medals for valor to his meticulous notes from more than 240 combat missions. Royer, who was 91 when he died in 2024, was born in Centre Hall and spent much of his youth in nearby Millheim. A serious man who remained active in his community, Royer was notoriously private. In his later years, he suffered complications linked to Agent Orange, a hazardous tactical herbicide used in Vietnam, and carried with him the weight of the missions he had flown — particularly the traumatic loss of members of his flight crew. Despite his silence, Royer meticulously documented his service, leaving behind maps, photographs and hand-written notes tucked away in his home. HUNTER SMITH/THE EXPRESS Kenneth's sons, Donald and Dennis, are pictured amidst their father’s memorabilia. After his passing, his sons began sorting through the memorabilia and uncovered, among other things, evidence of covert bombing campaigns in Laos and Cambodia, as well as personal records that added depth to their understanding of his life. Kenneth Royer enlisted in the Air Force on April 7, 1953, and completed basic training at a military installation in New York, where he passed the Aviation Cadet Entrance Examination. Later that year, he graduated from Lackland Air Force Base in Texas and began what would become a decorated, two-decade-long career that took him from the Korean Peninsula to the skies over Vietnam. During his service, Royer served as a radar navigator on more than 240 B-52 bombing missions — a tally almost unheard of among airmen of his era. Known for his precision, he performed complex calculations amid enemy fire to guide his crew through successful strikes against critical targets. After one mission, his son Donald J. Royer recalled, “The military police came out in a Jeep, got him from the plane and took him back to a conference room. They went over what his next mission was and gave him a half-hour before getting into another B-52 and flying.” Royer’s skill as a navigator earned him the respect of his fellow crew members and made him indispensable to his squadron. HUNTER SMITH/THE EXPRESS Various photos, medals, journals and other artifacts uncovered by the Royer family after Kenneth passed on Oct. 11, 2024 are shown. “I asked him one time, I said, ‘So, you’re that good?'” Donald said. “And he goes, ‘You put a dime in the backyard, guarantee I’ll hit it.'” Royer’s skill and steadiness in the sky earned him a long list of decorations over his 20 years of service. A multiple-time recipient of the Air Medal — conferred by executive order of the president — he received one for each tour and notable accomplishment. Among his other honors were the Air Force Commendation Medal, Combat Readiness Medal, Good Conduct Medal, National Defense Service Medal, Korean Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, United Nations Medal, Republic of Vietnam Campaign Medal, Presidential Unit Citation, Air Force Outstanding Unit Award, Air Force Longevity Service Award Ribbon, Air Force Organizational Excellence Award, and the Small Arms Expert Marksmanship Ribbon, among others. But his most prestigious honor came in 1972, when he was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross. On April 4 of that year, Royer demonstrated exceptional skill during aerial operations as a B-52 radar navigator over Southeast Asia. “On that date, while flying a critical bombing mission against a high-priority target, Colonel Royer’s aircraft encountered hostile fire immediately after making a successful weapons release,” the citation accompanying the award reads. “During the attack, Colonel Royer constantly kept his pilot advised of missile detonations and other aircraft positions, thereby dynamically assisting in the safe recovery of all aircraft and crews.” HUNTER SMITH/THE EXPRESS Various photos, medals, journals and other artifacts uncovered by the Royer family after Kenneth passed on Oct. 11, 2024 are shown. The award goes on to highlight his skill and dedication: “The professional competence, aerial skill and devotion to duty displayed by Colonel Royer reflect great credit upon himself and the United States Air Force.” “He got everybody back safe by keeping them apprised as to what was going on and where they were at,” said his daughter-in-law, Penny Royer, proudly. Though he was most well-regarded as a radar navigator, “the other aspect of his military career is that most of it was in the Strategic Air Command,” said one of his other sons, Dennis D. Royer. Throughout the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union held their fingers over the proverbial nuclear button. At each base, Dennis said, about six planes were usually pre-loaded with nuclear weapons. As part of his responsibilities, his father was prepared to respond to a nuclear attack at a moment’s notice. Dennis, who lived on base with his father, recalled one of the tensest moments of that era: the Cuban Missile Crisis. HUNTER SMITH/THE EXPRESS Various photos, medals, journals and other artifacts uncovered by the Royer family after Kenneth passed on Oct. 11, 2024 are shown. “During the Cuban Missile Crisis, they were at the end of the runway — engines running — waiting for takeoff,” he said. “What their targets were, who knows. But they were ready to wage nuclear war.” Thankfully, the U.S. and the Soviet Union didn’t come to blows, and Royer was able to conclude his career alive, having never deployed a nuclear weapon. Instead, near the end of his career, he reached a personal milestone: his 200th mission, when his wife, Lois Smith, joined him in the tower. “They were soulmates,” said Penny. “She was his driving force.” On that mission, Penny said. “She got on the radio and said, ‘Honey, I’m bringing you home.'” Having preceded him in death, Lois, Penny imagines, offered the same guidance on his final journey to the heavens that she gave him on his way down from them. Sign in to your Collider account Summary Generate a summary of this story follow Follow followed Followed Like Like Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap There is a lot to love about The Office , but at the top of that list is the ensemble cast. Though Michael Scott ( Steve Carell ) easily takes the lead role, the entire Dunder Mifflin staff is important in making the series the hilarious workplace comedy it is. No matter how small the role, each character sitting at a desk is a much-needed addition to the story, giving Michael a quirky staff to lead. With the likes of Stanley ( Leslie David Baker ), Kevin ( Brian Baumgartner ), Oscar ( Oscar Nuñez ), and Meredith ( Kate Flannery ), the office is filled out to reach its full potential, and each one is expertly cast. Yet one character wasn\'t supposed to be in the show at all. It\'s well known that the series used some of its writers onscreen, like Ryan ( B. J. Novak ) and Kelly ( Mindy Kaling ), but The Office pulled actors from elsewhere as well, including the casting department. That is how the character Phyllis made it into the show. Played by Phyllis Smith , the character became an integral part of The Office , sitting in the background for all nine seasons , but the story behind her casting is utterly unique. Smith never anticipated breaking into acting through The Office , but it is just the latest twist in her professional career, and her unexpected casting undoubtedly changed the series for the better. How Did Phyllis Smith Get a Part in \'The Office\'? Phyllis Smith as Phyllis Vance in The Office Image via NBC Like most casting choices, Smith\'s started in an audition, but oddly, she didn\'t know it was for her. Smith initially joined The Office as a casting associate , working with casting director Allison Jones . Smith explained on the Office Ladies podcast that she had been working in casting for some time, but the series director, Ken Kwapis , gave her an unusual opportunity. When pairing the actors for Jim ( John Krasinski ) , Dwight ( Rainn Wilson ), and Pam ( Jenna Fischer ) to see which prospective cast member had chemistry, Kwapis asked Smith to read for Pam. Smith was surprised but explained, "I wanted to do a good job, not for me but for the actors." After reading with Krasinski and an actor auditioning for Dwight, she was asked to read as Dwight with a different set of actors, rather than reading the part that she would eventually play. Smith didn\'t even hear about her role the traditional way. Telling the story on Office Ladies, she said, "Greg Daniels or no one ever said to me, \'Phyllis, do you want to be in the show?\'" Instead, Smith recalls that the casting office received an updated script that included a character with her name. Smith describes Jones asking if it was meant to be her Phyllis, though Smith herself never heard the answer. Instead, she knew she had the role later. Smith explained, "Wardrobe called and said, \'I understand you\'re playing the character of Phyllis.\' And I said, \'Yes, I am.\' Because I knew the union rules said if wardrobe called you or if you were sent the script, that constituted a work call. And so, when wardrobe called, I knew it was to be." Smith received a rare and unlikely opportunity with that call, and fortunately for The Office , she didn\'t hesitate to seize it. Posts By Kendall Myers Nov 1, 2025 Joining \'The Office\' Cast Wasn\'t Phyllis Smith\'s First Career Change Phyllis (Phyllis Smith) dancing with Darryl (Craig Robinson) in The Office Image via NBC Going from casting associate to actor may be a huge, unexpected shift, but it isn\'t the only time Smith\'s career path took a dramatic turn. Smith explained on another episode of the Office Ladies podcast that before working in casting, she performed in a traveling vaudeville burlesque show for several years, until they took the show to California to rework it. During the traveling break, Smith began performing in "The Captain\'s Crew Review" in Long Beach at Shoreline Village, but an injury forced Smith to make a change. Smith recalls, " I injured my knee doing a jump split at the end of the can-can . So that kind of ended my dancing career." From there, she became a receptionist at an aerospace defense company, but she went out on auditions. During one call for a part she didn\'t get, Smith told the casting director, "I think I might be good in casting." Soon enough, that casting director reached out to her, launching a 19-year career that only ended when The Office came along. Now, Smith is known not only as Phyllis in The Office , but also as Inside Out \'s Sadness , a character perfectly brought to life by Smith\'s voice. Smith\'s story is far from ordinary, but she has made an impressive career. Phyllis Became Integral to \'The Office\' While Phyllis may only have been added to the script after Smith impressed the director, she became a major part of the series for all nine seasons. No, she never serves as a lead in the way that many others do, but the secondary characters are part of what makes The Office so hilarious . After all, Michael needs to be in charge of someone, and Phyllis makes a unique addition to the series. Smith\'s portrayal as a seemingly shy sales rep who suddenly drops snarky one-liners turned her into a memorable character. Phyllis may look like a sweet, unassuming Dunder Mifflin veteran, but she has a mean streak, and it\'s hard not to laugh when the unsuspecting Phyllis drops a scathing remark like, "I\'m glad Michael\'s getting help. He has a lot of issues, and he\'s stupid." But that surprise is part of her charm. Between the occasional insults and dirty comments, Phyllis offers many jokes that slowly build her character into something fans never expected. Phyllis only had one line in the pilot , but she grew into an important character. Eventually, she got her own storylines, such as her marriage to Bob Vance ( Bobby Ray Shafer ) and her Party Planning Committee feud with Angela ( Angela Kinsey ). These storylines took her from the reserved woman who was often the subject of Michael\'s insensitive jokes to a bold character who refused to let others walk all over her. Phyllis blackmails Angela into giving her control of the parties, and responds to Karen\'s ( Rashida Jones ) insult to her husband with a sassy, "You\'ve a lot to learn about this town, sweetie." She even stands up to Michael in the Christmas episode , where she keeps her position as Santa despite Michael\'s fit. Though Phyllis wasn\'t a planned character, she played a compelling and realistic role in the series, and Smith\'s involvement was a large part of that. Without Phyllis Smith, The Office would never have created this hilarious character. All Rights Reserved A Major Office Actor Was Never Supposed To Be On The Show Calendar Every New Show Christmas Movies News TV Streaming Reviews Exclusives Features Newsletter Television Primetime TV Sitcom A Major Office Actor Was Never Supposed To Be On The Show By Joe Roberts Oct. 30, 2025 1:02 pm EST NBC "The Office" has long since cemented its standing as one of the great TV sitcoms, and a big part of its lasting appeal comes down to the characters. Even the lesser members of the ensemble were truly memorable, which was at least in part due to the excellent casting. Casting director Allison Jones brought together seasoned veterans with improv backgrounds alongside relative unknowns to create arguably one of the best TV casts ever assembled. But she also inadvertently provided "The Office" with a performer who was never actually supposed to be on the show. Phyllis Smith\'s Phyllis Vance (née Lapin) was with the series throughout its nine-season run and became a beloved member of the cast. The shy and reserved sales representative was never quite as uproariously funny as Steve Carell\'s Michael Scott or Rainn Wilson\'s Dwight Schrute. But she was still one of the best characters on "The Office" and often surprised with moments of pure, unadulterated sass that added a whole new dimension to the otherwise docile sales rep. Smith\'s thoroughly believable performance and her ability to play off the more outgoing performers in the cast were extra impressive, considering she wasn\'t even a full-time actor before playing Phyllis, and actually started out as part of the casting team led by Jones. Before "The Office," where she appeared until the series finale in season 9 , Smith worked as a casting associate on a handful of series, including "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman," "Curb Your Enthusiasm," and "Spin City." But during the casting process for "The Office," one of Smith\'s jobs was to read lines with the auditionees, and it turns out director Ken Kwapis liked her delivery so much that he pushed for the writers to create an entirely new character just for her. How Phyllis went from casting associate to a member of The Office cast NBC During an episode of the rewatch podcast "Office Ladies," hosted by Angela Kinsey and Jenna Fischer, Phyllis Smith went into detail about her career as a casting associate. After working as — of all things — a dancer in a vaudeville burlesque show, Smith injured her knee and found work as a receptionist. It was during this very "Office"-esque real-world job that she got called in to an audition, and while she didn\'t land the role, she did tell the casting director, "I think I might be good in casting." Soon after, she started working alongside that particular casting director and eventually interviewed to become Allison Jones\' associate. That led to her reading with the auditionees for "The Office." In a separate "Office Ladies" episode , Smith recalled to her former co-stars how she came to be cast as a member of the Dunder Mifflin team. "We were at the point in the casting process where we were pairing up the actors to see what their chemistry would be together," she explained. "I remember Ken Kwapis, the director, he was getting his coffee together, and he turned around to me and he said, \'Phyllis, I want you to read the character of Pam today. I went, what?" As Smith recalled, she had no idea why she was being asked to read with the "Office" prospects. "I remember a fax came through to our office with an updated script, and it had Phyllis in it," she said. "And Allison goes, \'Is this Phyllis? [...] But I never heard the answer.\'" Soon after, Smith suddenly found herself with a single line in the pilot episode of "The Office," and once she received a call from the wardrobe department, she grabbed the opportunity. Phyllis charmed an Office director with her down-to-earth manner NBC Ken Kwapis, who directed the pilot episode of "The Office" and went on to oversee several more installments across nine seasons, clearly saw something in Phyllis Smith during the casting process, and it was an inspired move to bring her into the cast. During a Reddit AMA, the director said he recommended her to showrunner/creator Greg Daniels after being taken by her "down-to-earth vibe" and her "sincerity." That certainly translated to the show itself and helped Phyllis become one of the most beloved members of the original ensemble. As such, she\'s an "Office" character who wouldn\'t be out of place on the spin-off, "The Paper," and with her husband Bob Vance (Robert R. Shafer) appearing in the premiere episode to offer an update on Dunder Mifflin, it doesn\'t seem entirely out of the question. Meanwhile, Smith herself has continued to work as an actor in the years since "The Office" ended, most notably voicing Sadness in Disney\'s "Inside Out" movies. She also played Betty Broderick-Allen in 12 episodes of Netflix\'s "The OA" before its cancellation in 2019 , and appeared in three episodes of the ABC sitcom "Trophy Wife." But she\'ll always have a special fondness for the show that turned her into an actor in the first place. As Smith said in a message sent to the "Office Ladies" hosts, "I loved every minute of being in \'The Office\' for nine years. It changed my life in a positive, good way. It gave me a career, a new career when I never even believed acting was ever going to happen for me [...] I really, truly loved every moment, and I still miss it." The idea of combining the positions came after Treasurer Jamie Longtine expressed a desire to return to her former position of deputy treasurer. After research showed at least three other Montana counties have combined the treasurer and clerk/recorder, on Monday afternoon County commissioners held a public hearing on the idea. “At first we didn’t really want to do this, but after looking into it more, we felt more ok with the idea,” Commissioner Ross Butcher said, adding the County is simultaneously advertising for someone to fill the position of treasurer until the next election in 2026. “I don’t know that my mind’s made up which is the best way,” Butcher said. Commissioner Jennifer Saunders said the position is being advertised in the News-Argus and on the internet job website Indeed, and on social media. “We’ve had a few inquiries but no actual applications yet,” she said. If the commissioners were to vote to combine the positions, they must do so before Feb. 10 because of deadlines related to the 2026 elections. “The person needs to know what position they are running for in order to file — is it treasurer or a combined position,” Butcher said. Should the proposal to combine positions be approved, the County’s Finance Director Neal Tucek would be responsible for the financial transactions, while the Clerk/Recorder/Treasurer would be in charge of running both departments. Clerk and Recorder Janel Tucek said she hopes a person comes forward to fill the Treasurer’s position, but the county needs a plan in case that does not happen. “I get that this is not ideal. I’d love to have a treasurer with an accounting degree. But this is the idea if that doesn’t happen,” she said. “It’s a backup plan if no one applies for the job,” Saunders said. What could go wrong? Retired Clerk of Court Phyllis Smith told the commissioners her biggest concern is the possibility for financial deception. “How are we going to do the checks and balances between the departments,” Smith asked. Neal Tucek said he and the Clerk and Recorder are developing a system of daily checks that both would need to sign off on. Tucek said that would help prevent embezzling, such as happened once before many years ago. “There are lots of internal controls in place now,” he said. “We are also reaching out to other counties that have combined these positions to see how they do it. I am asking those questions.” Resident Shannon Ruckman said her concern is the impact on customer service that combining offices might have. “I’d hate to see the Treasurer’s side put a kiosk out to ask the public to pay their taxes online,” Ruckman said, adding she would rather work with a real person that deal with an electronic device. “I’m thinking about the employees,” said former Treasurer’s office employee Mary Beth Roy. “You can do what you want at the top. What are you doing to help employees to feel happy and motivated. It’s about wages.” Retired Superintendent of Schools Shirley Barrick said she was concerned about workloads. “Every other November you have elections and taxes. Consolidating would mean one person doing two jobs that are very, very important. There’s going to have to be more help for both offices.” More opportunity to comment After hearing residents’ concerns, Butcher said he would delay closing the public hearing. “By law, if I close the hearing we only have five days before we have to make a decision,” Butcher said. “I am continuing the hearing to our next meeting.” The next scheduled meeting of the County commissioners is Wednesday, Nov. 19 at 5:15 p.m. in the commissioners office on the second floor of the courthouse. Col. Joanne Hirst discussed, on Nov. 10, her life as a member of the U.S. Army Reserves as the guest speaker at the annual Crystal River Woman’s Club’s Veteran’s Luncheon for Military Women. Margo Wilson / Chronicle correspondent If Joanne Hirst had her way, every teen upon graduating from high school would join the military. Not a community service program. Not college. Not the family business. The military. In an interview and at a luncheon honoring female veterans, Hirst spoke about her 36 years as a member of the U.S. Army Reserve. She retired in 2011 as a lieutenant colonel and a nurse practitioner. Her life wasn’t easy, and, in some ways, her military service made it more difficult. But in many ways, her service made her life more interesting, focused and easier. “There is not a child mature enough to go straight into college,” she said in the interview. As a member of the Female Veterans Network of Citrus County, Hirst visits schools as part of the Citrus County School District’s Veterans in the Classroom program. And she tells of encountering a student who said his occupational goal was “to flip burgers.” Others tell her they want to be tattoo artists or nail technicians. But these aren’t jobs that students can count on to carry them through their lifetimes, as Hirst sees it. “They need structure to grow up and they’re not getting it at home,” she said. “They need regular structure and guidance. They need someone to tell them to pick up their dirty underwear.” Moreover, the military has “a job for everyone,” according to Hirst. What’s more, the military will train you in many different areas and also will pay for you to attend college. That’s how Hirst got to be a nurse practitioner. Photos by Margo Wilson / Chronicle correspondent A single mom’s path At the Crystal River Woman’s Club’s annual Veteran’s Luncheon for Military Women, guest speaker Hirst told how she went from being a 24-year-old single mom clerk typist, working at a hospital, to enlisting as an Army reservist in 1975 when she heard about the benefits some reservist coworkers were receiving. “I was ready to go back to school,” she said. She joined the Reserves as a corporal and clerk-typist but after a couple of years, signed up for a medic’s course. Next, she had the opportunity to study to be a licensed practical nurse, so she did. Then came an associate degree in applied science, and then she studied to be a registered nurse. Her Bachelor of Science degree in nursing followed. She said her “thirst for knowledge” spurred her to pursue her education. Then, one day, she received information from her alma mater, SUNY Polytechnic Institute of Utica, New York, that the school was starting a master’s degree program for nurse practitioners. Hirst signed up for that, too. “Finally, I knew what I wanted to do when I grew up,” she said. She said she started her educational pursuits in 1978, when her son, Brian, was 8. When she graduated as a nurse practitioner in 1997, Brian brought his 2-day-old daughter, Sabine, to the commencement, straight from the hospital. Nursing and engineering graduates cradled Sabine and passed her around as part of the festivities. Military and civilian service All the time Hirst was in the Reserves, she held civilian jobs, too. She worked in various positions at the Schoharie County Health Department in New York. She was an RN on a hospital surgery floor. As a nurse practitioner, she worked at a doctor’s office that was affiliated with a hospital. There, she counseled young women who might be having their first OB-GYN exam or helped seniors who might need home health care or transportation. While she was attending SUNY Polytech, she’d leave work about 4:30 p.m. and then drive over an hour twice a week, “following the snowplow,” to get to her classes starting at 6 p.m. When she was home, she frequently had a book in her hand. She told of attending Brian’s ballgames, nose poked in a book, and relying on others to tell her, “Brian’s up to bat.” Even though her attention was split, “I was always present,” she said. “I’m a good mom.” She credits her late husband, Charles, whom she met at her military unit’s Christmas party in 1975 and married in 1978, for pitching in when she couldn’t. Charles also was a reservist and a licensed practical nurse, as well as a mechanic and electrical specialist. Serving abroad Although Hirst spent many of her years as a nurse in New York State, as a reservist, she served at Army humanitarian clinics in Guatemala and Honduras in the late 1990s, seeing up to 1,400 people a day. She also supervised clinics in Germany in 2004-05 and ended her military career at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, helping launch the Wounded Warrior project. Her time at humanitarian clinics in Guatemala and Honduras left an impression. She told of how villagers would walk for hours to attend the clinics. “We’re in Crystal River,” she said. “It would be like if they walked in from Inverness or Inglis.” One villager rode in on a Brahman cow and somehow, the cow stepped on the woman’s foot and broke it. A man put the woman on his horse and led the horse to the hospital, Hirst said. Other villagers would have bacterial infections, and the doctors and nurses would give medication to clear up the infections. But when the villagers returned to their villages and the two- to three-week clinic had moved on, the villagers most likely were reinfected by the water or whatever source initially had caused their infection. The medical personnel served one remote village that a few months later was destroyed in a hurricane, and many of the people whom the medical people had treated died in the storm. Still, being able to care for others was a privilege, according to Hirst, who describes herself as “a nurturer …. I wanted to be a nurse ever since second grade.” Nurses, she said, “see everything. We have the information. We watch everything …. And, we have a smile.” Facing challenges Hirst is one who keeps smiling, even though she’s faced her share of difficulties. She is a three-time cancer survivor. Her husband passed away in 2018. But Hirst keeps going. “I try to be a mentor to other women,” she said. As historian for the Female Veterans Network, she’s found a supportive group that “is my lifeline, we are family …. “I have an excellent system with Female Veterans Network, and that’s what you need. You need to develop that, one way or another. Even if you’re in a shelter, they will help you …. There is always hope.” The Female Veterans Network can be reached at 352-628-6481. The Crystal River Woman’s Club can be reached at 352-795-5488. At Monday’s luncheon, club President Becky Culver gave the invocation. Crystal River High School’s Navy Junior Reserve Officers Training Corps presented the colors. Army veteran Carole Jasler led the National Anthem and the singing of military songs. Woman’s Club member Margie Harper led the blessing, and the club’s first vice president and event organizer Leslie Martineau welcomed those attending. Libby Wentzell was in charge of door prizes. Ana Segovia, district aide with U.S. Rep. Gus Bilirakis, welcomed the group. Hirst received a quilt from the Rainbow Quilters of Citrus Springs. Margo Wilson / Chronicle correspondent Nonagenarian Phyllis Smith spoke briefly about serving as a real-life “Rosie the Riveter” during World War II, making manifolds for B-29 bombers at a factory in Elmira, New York. She was 16 when she started working at the factory, having to quit school to help support her family. She’s been a member of the Woman’s Club for 27 years. Martineau said women like Smith helped open the doors for women to work in many fields. “You were a revolutionary and you didn’t know it,” she said. Also at the luncheon, the Women of the Moose of Dunnellon Lodge 2308, presented the Woman’s Club with a check for $500 from the Moose’s Valued Veterans Committee. Alma Whitman, senior regent of the Women of the Moose, said the Moose wanted to acknowledge the contributions the Woman’s Club makes and to also help out a bit, since the club’s building was twice damaged by hurricanes recently. Though Michael Scott ( Steve Carell ) easily takes the lead role, the entire Dunder Mifflin staff is important in making the series the hilarious workplace comedy it is. No matter how small the role, each character sitting at a desk is a much-needed addition to the story, giving Michael a quirky staff to lead. With the likes of Stanley ( Leslie David Baker ), Kevin ( Brian Baumgartner ), Oscar ( Oscar Nuñez ), and Meredith ( Kate Flannery ), the office is filled out to reach its full potential, and each one is expertly cast. Yet one character wasn\'t supposed to be in the show at all. It\'s well known that the series used some of its writers onscreen, like Ryan ( B. J. Novak ) and Kelly ( Mindy Kaling ), but The Office pulled actors from elsewhere as well, including the casting department. That is how the character Phyllis made it into the show. Played by Phyllis Smith , the character became an integral part of The Office , sitting in the background for all nine seasons , but the story behind her casting is utterly unique. Smith never anticipated breaking into acting through The Office , but it is just the latest twist in her professional career, and her unexpected casting undoubtedly changed the series for the better. How Did Phyllis Smith Get a Part in \'The Office\'? Phyllis Smith as Phyllis Vance in The Office Image via NBC Like most casting choices, Smith\'s started in an audition, but oddly, she didn\'t know it was for her. Smith initially joined The Office as a casting associate , working with casting director Allison Jones . Smith explained on the Office Ladies podcast that she had been working in casting for some time, but the series director, Ken Kwapis , gave her an unusual opportunity. When pairing the actors for Jim ( John Krasinski ) , Dwight ( Rainn Wilson ), and Pam ( Jenna Fischer ) to see which prospective cast member had chemistry, Kwapis asked Smith to read for Pam. Smith was surprised but explained, "I wanted to do a good job, not for me but for the actors." After reading with Krasinski and an actor auditioning for Dwight, she was asked to read as Dwight with a different set of actors, rather than reading the part that she would eventually play. Smith didn\'t even hear about her role the traditional way. Telling the story on Office Ladies, she said, "Greg Daniels or no one ever said to me, \'Phyllis, do you want to be in the show?\'" Instead, Smith recalls that the casting office received an updated script that included a character with her name. Smith describes Jones asking if it was meant to be her Phyllis, though Smith herself never heard the answer. Instead, she knew she had the role later. Smith explained, "Wardrobe called and said, \'I understand you\'re playing the character of Phyllis.\' And I said, \'Yes, I am.\' Because I knew the union rules said if wardrobe called you or if you were sent the script, that constituted a work call. And so, when wardrobe called, I knew it was to be." Smith received a rare and unlikely opportunity with that call, and fortunately for The Office , she didn\'t hesitate to seize it. Posts By Kendall Myers Nov 1, 2025 Joining \'The Office\' Cast Wasn\'t Phyllis Smith\'s First Career Change Phyllis (Phyllis Smith) dancing with Darryl (Craig Robinson) in The Office Image via NBC Going from casting associate to actor may be a huge, unexpected shift, but it isn\'t the only time Smith\'s career path took a dramatic turn. Smith explained on another episode of the Office Ladies podcast that before working in casting, she performed in a traveling vaudeville burlesque show for several years, until they took the show to California to rework it. During the traveling break, Smith began performing in "The Captain\'s Crew Review" in Long Beach at Shoreline Village, but an injury forced Smith to make a change. Smith recalls, " I injured my knee doing a jump split at the end of the can-can . So that kind of ended my dancing career." From there, she became a receptionist at an aerospace defense company, but she went out on auditions. During one call for a part she didn\'t get, Smith told the casting director, "I think I might be good in casting." Soon enough, that casting director reached out to her, launching a 19-year career that only ended when The Office came along. Now, Smith is known not only as Phyllis in The Office , but also as Inside Out \'s Sadness , a character perfectly brought to life by Smith\'s voice. Smith\'s story is far from ordinary, but she has made an impressive career. Phyllis Became Integral to \'The Office\' While Phyllis may only have been added to the script after Smith impressed the director, she became a major part of the series for all nine seasons. No, she never serves as a lead in the way that many others do, but the secondary characters are part of what makes The Office so hilarious . After all, Michael needs to be in charge of someone, and Phyllis makes a unique addition to the series. Smith\'s portrayal as a seemingly shy sales rep who suddenly drops snarky one-liners turned her into a memorable character. Phyllis may look like a sweet, unassuming Dunder Mifflin veteran, but she has a mean streak, and it\'s hard not to laugh when the unsuspecting Phyllis drops a scathing remark like, "I\'m glad Michael\'s getting help. He has a lot of issues, and he\'s stupid." But that surprise is part of her charm. Between the occasional insults and dirty comments, Phyllis offers many jokes that slowly build her character into something fans never expected. Phyllis only had one line in the pilot , but she grew into an important character. Eventually, she got her own storylines, such as her marriage to Bob Vance ( Bobby Ray Shafer ) and her Party Planning Committee feud with Angela ( Angela Kinsey ). These storylines took her from the reserved woman who was often the subject of Michael\'s insensitive jokes to a bold character who refused to let others walk all over her. Phyllis blackmails Angela into giving her control of the parties, and responds to Karen\'s ( Rashida Jones ) insult to her husband with a sassy, "You\'ve a lot to learn about this town, sweetie." She even stands up to Michael in the Christmas episode , where she keeps her position as Santa despite Michael\'s fit. Though Phyllis wasn\'t a planned character, she played a compelling and realistic role in the series, and Smith\'s involvement was a large part of that. Without Phyllis Smith, The Office would never have created this hilarious character.
